One illustrative implementation of the invention concerns a technique for estimating the hydraulic permeability of rocks within an underground region. The technique includes measuring in place and/or deriving by calculation one or more independent seismic velocities of rocks at various positions in the subsurface region. Based on those measured seismic velocities, at least one lithological unit within the subsurface region is identified.

For the identified lithological unit, one or more rock samples are obtained from at least one location in the subsurface region. The porosity and permeability of the rock sample are then measured as stress-dependent properties. In addition, one or more independent seismic velocities of the rock sample are measured and/or calculated as functions of stress.

The method further involves determining the stiff porosity and compliant porosity of the rock sample, using those stiff and compliant porosities to calculate numerical parameters for a selected analytical permeability model, and also calculating parameters for a selected analytical model describing an elastic-compliance property of the rock.

Stiff and compliant porosity values are then determined for multiple additional locations in the subsurface region. Finally, the permeability of rocks associated with the identified lithological unit is calculated both for the sampled location in the subsurface region and for the multiple additional locations in that region.
outputs.L3:
The method determines the hydraulic permeability of rocks in a subsurface region by using in-situ seismic velocity measurements, or seismic velocities calculated from subsurface data. These seismic velocities provide information about the elastic properties of the rocks and are used as an indirect indicator of rock structure, pore geometry, and fluid-flow capacity.

First, seismic velocities are measured or otherwise obtained at multiple locations within the subsurface region. The measured velocities are then analyzed to identify lithological units, meaning regions of rock that share similar geological and mechanical characteristics. Different rock types typically exhibit different seismic velocity ranges, so the velocity data can be used to distinguish one lithological unit from another and to map their distribution within the subsurface.

Rock samples are then obtained from the subsurface region, preferably from locations representative of the identified lithological units. These samples are tested in the laboratory to determine key petrophysical and elastic properties. The tests measure porosity, hydraulic permeability, and seismic velocities under varying stress conditions. Measuring these properties as functions of stress allows the method to account for changes that occur at depth, where rocks are subjected to different confining pressures and effective stresses.

Using the laboratory measurements, the rock porosity is separated into stiff porosity and compliant porosity components. Stiff porosity refers to pore space that is relatively insensitive to stress changes, while compliant porosity refers to cracks, microfractures, or other pore features that close or deform significantly under stress. These porosity components are computed from the sample data and used to calibrate analytical models that relate permeability and elastic compliance to rock structure and stress state.

Once calibrated, the analytical permeability model and elastic-compliance model are applied to the subsurface region. For locations where samples were collected, the models can be used to compute permeability values directly from the measured rock properties and seismic velocities. For other locations within the same identified lithological unit, the calibrated relationship between seismic velocity, porosity structure, stress, and permeability is used to estimate rock permeability without requiring a physical sample from each location.

In this way, the method provides a framework for estimating hydraulic permeability throughout a subsurface lithological unit using a combination of seismic velocity data, laboratory measurements, and calibrated rock-physics models. This enables permeability to be evaluated not only at sampled points, but also across broader regions where seismic data are available.
outputs.L4:
A method is provided for determining the hydraulic permeability of subsurface rock formations using a combination of in-situ seismic measurements, lithological information, laboratory rock-sample data, and analytical rock-physics modeling. The method is intended to estimate how readily fluids can flow through rocks at depth, including at locations where no direct core or plug permeability measurements are available.

In one implementation, seismic velocity data are obtained from a subsurface region of interest. The seismic data may include compressional-wave velocity, shear-wave velocity, or both, and may be derived from borehole logging, surface seismic surveys, vertical seismic profiling, cross-well seismic measurements, or other in-situ geophysical measurements. These velocity data provide information about the elastic properties of the rock while it remains under natural subsurface pressure and stress conditions.

The subsurface region is also classified according to lithology. For example, the rock may be identified as sandstone, carbonate, shale, siltstone, or another lithological type. This classification may be made using well logs, core descriptions, cuttings, mineralogical analysis, seismic interpretation, or combinations of these sources. The lithological classification is used to group rocks that are expected to share similar pore structures, mechanical behavior, and permeability relationships.

Representative rock samples from the lithological unit are then analyzed in the laboratory. These samples may be subjected to confining pressures or effective stresses that simulate subsurface conditions. During testing, physical properties such as porosity, permeability, density, compressional velocity, shear velocity, or elastic moduli may be measured. By performing measurements under stress, the method accounts for the fact that pore spaces, cracks, and microfractures can close or deform at depth, thereby changing both seismic velocity and hydraulic permeability.

The measured rock-sample data are used to calibrate an analytical model of the pore system. In particular, the model distinguishes between stiff porosity and compliant porosity. Stiff porosity refers to pore volume that is relatively resistant to closure under increasing stress, such as well-connected intergranular pores or rigid pore spaces within the rock framework. Compliant porosity refers to pore volume associated with cracks, microfractures, grain contacts, or other thin and easily deformable pore features that may close significantly under stress. Because compliant pores can strongly affect seismic velocity while contributing differently to fluid flow, separating these pore types improves the relationship between elastic properties and permeability.

Using the analytical model, the in-situ seismic velocity data are converted into estimates of pore structure parameters for the lithological unit. The model may determine the relative amounts of stiff and compliant porosity, the stress-dependent porosity state, or other parameters related to pore geometry and connectivity. These parameters are then used to calculate hydraulic permeability. The calculation may be performed at multiple subsurface locations where seismic velocity data and lithological classification are available, even if physical rock samples were collected only from a limited number of points.

As a result, the method provides a way to extend permeability estimates away from wells, cores, or other directly sampled locations. Once calibrated for a particular lithological unit, the method can be applied throughout that unit to generate a spatial distribution of permeability. This distribution may be used in reservoir characterization, groundwater studies, geothermal assessment, carbon storage evaluation, hydrocarbon production planning, or other subsurface flow applications.

The approach improves permeability prediction by combining direct laboratory measurements with field-scale seismic observations and a physically based description of pore compressibility. Rather than relying solely on empirical correlations between porosity and permeability, the method incorporates the effects of lithology, stress, elastic velocity, and pore type. This enables more reliable estimation of rock flow properties under actual subsurface conditions and provides permeability values for regions where direct permeability measurements are unavailable.

An exemplary embodiment is a specific example used to explain how an invention, concept, system, or method may be implemented in practice. It is commonly used in technical descriptions, patents, product documentation, and engineering materials to illustrate one possible version of an idea without limiting it to that exact form.

For example, if a document describes a new type of smart lighting system, an exemplary embodiment might include a lamp, a motion sensor, a wireless controller, and a mobile application. This example helps readers understand how the system can work, but it does not mean the invention is restricted only to that arrangement. Other embodiments may use different sensors, communication methods, or control devices.

The purpose of an exemplary embodiment is to make an abstract idea clearer and more practical. By presenting a concrete example, the description becomes easier to understand, test, and reproduce. However, the term also leaves room for variations, improvements, and alternative designs.

In short, an exemplary embodiment serves as a representative model. It demonstrates one possible way to carry out an idea while allowing flexibility for other implementations.

counterfactuals.output:
## Exemplary Embodiment

In one exemplary embodiment, a computer-implemented method is provided for determining hydraulic permeability of a subsurface rock formation using seismic velocity data, rock physics measurements, and an analytical permeability model. The method may be performed by one or more processors executing instructions stored in a non-transitory computer-readable medium, and may be applied to a reservoir interval penetrated by one or more wells and imaged by surface seismic, borehole seismic, cross-well seismic, or any combination thereof.

### Data Acquisition and Conditioning

Seismic data are acquired over a subsurface region containing a formation of interest. The seismic data may include pre-stack seismic gathers, post-stack seismic volumes, vertical seismic profile data, cross-well seismic data, or combinations thereof. The seismic data are processed to obtain one or more elastic property volumes, including at least compressional-wave velocity \(V_p\), shear-wave velocity \(V_s\), acoustic impedance, shear impedance, density, Poisson’s ratio, bulk modulus, shear modulus, or combinations thereof.

In one implementation, pre-stack seismic inversion is performed to generate three-dimensional volumes of \(V_p\), \(V_s\), and density \(\rho\). In another implementation, seismic attributes derived from amplitude variation with offset or angle are inverted to estimate elastic moduli. The elastic property volumes may be depth converted and registered to well log data. The method may further include conditioning the seismic velocity data by filtering, anisotropy correction, pressure correction, temperature correction, fluid substitution, upscaling, or calibration against well logs.

Rock physics measurements are obtained from core samples, cuttings, sidewall cores, well logs, laboratory measurements, or combinations thereof. The rock physics measurements may include porosity, mineral composition, clay volume, grain density, bulk density, compressional and shear velocities measured under confining pressure, pore fluid properties, cementation exponent, tortuosity factor, specific surface area, pore throat size distribution, capillary pressure, nuclear magnetic resonance data, mercury injection capillary pressure data, and measured permeability values. These measurements are used to calibrate a rock physics relationship linking seismic velocity to pore structure parameters that control hydraulic permeability.

### Rock Physics Transformation

A rock physics model is selected for the formation of interest. The model may relate seismic velocity to porosity, effective stress, lithology, pore shape, cementation, sorting, coordination number, or pore connectivity. In one embodiment, the model estimates porosity \(\phi\) from seismic velocity using a calibrated velocity-porosity relationship. For example, the compressional-wave velocity may be represented as a function of porosity, mineral moduli, fluid moduli, and effective pressure:

\[
V_p = \sqrt{\frac{K_{\text{sat}} + \frac{4}{3}\mu_{\text{sat}}}{\rho_{\text{sat}}}}
\]

where \(K_{\text{sat}}\) is the saturated bulk modulus, \(\mu_{\text{sat}}\) is the saturated shear modulus, and \(\rho_{\text{sat}}\) is the saturated bulk density. The saturated bulk modulus may be obtained from a dry-frame modulus and a fluid substitution relationship, such as a Gassmann-type relationship:

\[
K_{\text{sat}} = K_{\text{dry}} +
\frac{\left(1-\frac{K_{\text{dry}}}{K_m}\right)^2}
{\frac{\phi}{K_f}+\frac{1-\phi}{K_m}-\frac{K_{\text{dry}}}{K_m^2}}
\]

where \(K_m\) is the mineral bulk modulus and \(K_f\) is the pore fluid bulk modulus. The dry-frame modulus \(K_{\text{dry}}\) may be determined from an effective medium model, a contact cement model, a friable sand model, a stiff sand model, a critical porosity model, or an empirically calibrated rock physics template.

In another embodiment, both \(V_p\) and \(V_s\) are used to estimate porosity and pore geometry. The ratio \(V_p/V_s\), Poisson’s ratio, or elastic impedance may be used to distinguish lithology, clay content, cementation, or fluid effects. The transformation may generate one or more intermediate rock parameters, including porosity \(\phi\), clay fraction, carbonate fraction, pore aspect ratio, coordination number, cement volume, effective pressure, sorting index, or pore connectivity index.

The rock physics transformation may be calibrated by minimizing a mismatch between predicted velocities and measured velocities obtained from core plugs or well logs. Calibration parameters may include cementation exponent, critical porosity, mineral moduli, pore aspect ratio, coordination number, pressure sensitivity coefficients, or lithology-dependent constants. The calibrated transformation is then applied to the seismic velocity volume to generate a spatial distribution of porosity and related pore-structure parameters throughout the subsurface region.

### Analytical Permeability Modeling

An analytical permeability model is applied to the rock physics-derived parameters to determine hydraulic permeability. In one embodiment, the permeability \(k\) is calculated using a Kozeny-Carman-type expression:

\[
k = \frac{C}{S_v^2} \frac{\phi^3}{(1-\phi)^2}
\]

where \(S_v\) is specific surface area per unit grain volume and \(C\) is a calibration factor associated with pore tortuosity and pore shape. The specific surface area may be obtained from core measurements, mineralogical data, nuclear magnetic resonance measurements, grain size analysis, or a lithology-dependent empirical relationship. The calibration factor may be determined from measured permeability values from core plugs or formation tests.

In another embodiment, permeability is determined using an analytical model that includes pore throat radius:

\[
k = A \frac{\phi r_t^2}{\tau}
\]

where \(r_t\) is an effective pore throat radius, \(\tau\) is tortuosity, and \(A\) is a geometric constant. The pore throat radius may be estimated from rock physics measurements, capillary pressure data, mercury injection measurements, or a seismic-derived pore structure index. Tortuosity may be represented as a function of porosity, cementation exponent, clay volume, or pore connectivity.

In a further embodiment, the permeability model incorporates a critical porosity or percolation threshold. For example:

\[
k = k_0 \left(\frac{\phi-\phi_c}{1-\phi_c}\right)^n
\]

for \(\phi > \phi_c\), where \(\phi_c\) is a connectivity or percolation threshold, \(k_0\) is a scale factor, and \(n\) is an exponent calibrated using rock physics and permeability measurements. For \(\phi \leq \phi_c\), permeability may be assigned a low limiting value or determined using a separate microporosity model.

In another embodiment, an analytical permeability expression combines porosity, velocity-derived stiffness, and pore connectivity:

\[
k = B \, \phi^\alpha \left(\frac{V_{\text{ref}}}{V_p}\right)^\beta C_p
\]

where \(B\), \(\alpha\), and \(\beta\) are calibrated coefficients, \(V_{\text{ref}}\) is a reference velocity for the lithology, and \(C_p\) is a pore connectivity factor derived from rock physics measurements or estimated from \(V_p\), \(V_s\), density, and lithology. The connectivity factor may be reduced in cemented or clay-rich intervals and increased in well-sorted, connected pore systems.

### Integration of Seismic and Rock Physics Constraints

The seismic-derived permeability may be constrained using well-based measurements. In one embodiment, core permeability measurements are upscaled to seismic scale and compared with model-predicted permeability at corresponding well locations. A calibration procedure adjusts one or more parameters of the analytical permeability model to reduce error between predicted and measured permeability. The calibration may be lithology-specific, facies-specific, stratigraphic-zone-specific, pressure-dependent, or fluid-dependent.

The method may include classifying the subsurface volume into rock types or hydraulic flow units before calculating permeability. Rock types may be determined from seismic attributes, elastic properties, well logs, depositional facies, mineral composition, or clustering of rock physics parameters. Each rock type may be assigned a respective analytical permeability model or respective calibration constants. For example, clean sandstone, shaly sandstone, carbonate mudstone, vuggy carbonate, fractured carbonate, and tight siltstone may each have different model parameters.

In one implementation, the method comprises the following operations:

1. receiving seismic velocity data representative of a subsurface formation;
2. receiving rock physics measurements associated with the formation;
3. calibrating a rock physics model using the rock physics measurements;
4. applying the calibrated rock physics model to the seismic velocity data to estimate porosity and at least one pore-structure parameter;
5. selecting an analytical permeability model based on lithology, facies, or rock type;
6. calculating hydraulic permeability from the estimated porosity and pore-structure parameter;
7. generating a permeability volume or map for the subsurface formation; and
8. outputting the permeability volume or map for reservoir characterization, well placement, flow simulation, or production forecasting.

### Uncertainty Estimation

In some embodiments, uncertainty in the determined permeability is quantified. Uncertainty may arise from seismic inversion uncertainty, velocity measurement error, lithology uncertainty, fluid uncertainty, pressure effects, scale differences between core and seismic measurements, or uncertainty in analytical model parameters. The method may propagate uncertainty using Monte Carlo simulation, Bayesian inversion, ensemble modeling, linearized error propagation, geostatistical simulation, or combinations thereof.

For example, a plurality of realizations of \(V_p\), \(V_s\), density, porosity, pore throat radius, tortuosity, and calibration coefficients may be generated. The analytical permeability model is applied to each realization to produce a plurality of permeability realizations. Statistical measures, including mean permeability, median permeability, standard deviation, probability of exceeding a threshold permeability, or percentile maps, may be generated and displayed.

### Output and Use

The resulting hydraulic permeability values may be stored as a three-dimensional permeability volume, a two-dimensional map, a stratigraphic grid property, a reservoir simulation grid property, or a well planning attribute. The permeability volume may be displayed on a graphical user interface together with seismic data, well trajectories, structural horizons, faults, facies models, or reservoir simulation results.

In one embodiment, the determined permeability is used to identify high-permeability flow pathways, low-permeability baffles, sealing intervals, sweet spots for drilling, zones favorable for hydraulic fracturing, or regions of enhanced injectivity. The permeability may also be used as input to a reservoir simulator, basin model, groundwater flow model, carbon dioxide sequestration model, geothermal reservoir model, or hydrocarbon production forecasting system.

### Example System Implementation

An exemplary system includes a data storage device, one or more processors, and a display. The data storage device stores seismic velocity data, rock physics measurements, well log data, and executable instructions. The one or more processors execute the instructions to calibrate a rock physics model, estimate porosity and pore-structure parameters from the seismic velocity data, apply an analytical permeability model, and generate a permeability representation of the subsurface formation. The display presents the permeability representation to a user.

The system may further include an inversion module configured to derive elastic properties from seismic data, a rock physics module configured to transform elastic properties into pore-scale parameters, a permeability module configured to calculate hydraulic permeability using an analytical model, an uncertainty module configured to generate confidence intervals or probability maps, and an output module configured to export permeability values to a reservoir modeling or simulation platform.

### Illustrative Workflow

In an illustrative application, pre-stack seismic data are inverted to obtain \(V_p\), \(V_s\), and density volumes over a sandstone reservoir. Core plug measurements provide porosity, grain size, specific surface area, and laboratory permeability. A rock physics template is calibrated using the core and well log data to relate seismic velocity to porosity and cementation. The calibrated template is applied to the seismic velocity volume to estimate porosity and a cementation index throughout the reservoir.

A Kozeny-Carman-type permeability model is then parameterized using the measured specific surface area and core permeability. The cementation index modifies tortuosity in the permeability equation so that more cemented intervals are assigned lower permeability at equivalent porosity. The resulting permeability volume identifies laterally continuous high-permeability fairways and low-permeability barriers. The volume is exported to a reservoir simulator to improve prediction of fluid flow and production performance.

In another illustrative application, the formation comprises carbonate rocks having interparticle porosity, moldic porosity, and vuggy porosity. Seismic \(V_p/V_s\), impedance, and density are used to classify carbonate pore types. A pore-type-dependent analytical permeability model is selected for each classified region. For interparticle porosity, permeability is calculated using a pore throat radius model. For vuggy porosity, permeability is modified by a connectivity factor derived from seismic-scale heterogeneity attributes and calibrated against well test permeability. The resulting permeability model distinguishes isolated vugs from connected vuggy flow zones.

The foregoing exemplary embodiments are illustrative and not limiting. Variations may include different seismic attributes, different rock physics models, different analytical permeability relationships, different calibration techniques, and different output formats while remaining within the scope of determining hydraulic permeability from seismic velocity data, rock physics measurements, and analytical permeability modeling.
